Title: A Novel Elliptical‐Shaped UWB Two‐Port MIMO Antenna With Enhanced Isolation for Wireless Application

Te requirement for increased spectrum efciency, greater connection dependability, and high data rates has been exacerbated by the
rapid advancement of wireless technology. A potential solution to these requirements is the integration of ultrawideband (UWB)
technology with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. Te suggested antenna structure combines the merits of the UWB
technology, including low power consumption and a wide frequency bandwidth, with the spatial diversity of MIMO. Te UWB antenna
design is created by incorporating an elliptical shape structure into the circular monopole patch. To further improve the bandwidth,
a square shape cut is introduced on the partial ground surface. A two-element MIMO structure is designed by duplicating the UWB
antenna in parallel having a distance of 0.15λ, where wavelength is computed at 4.6GHz. Te fabricated structure has a size of
21.5× 34×1.6mm3. Te FR4 substrate was employed to construct the UWB MIMO antenna. Te introduction of a caterpillar-shaped
parasitic element between the antenna element results in isolation levels greater than 20dB and operating bandwidth ranging from 4.6 to
13.6 GHz. Te measured maximum gain was 7.3 dBi at 13GHz in full wave simulations and experiments. Additionally, an analysis is
conducted on the diversity parameters. Te designed antenna demonstrates a comparatively good performance.
Keywords: defected ground structure (DGS); isolation; MIMO; parasitic element; ultrawideband
1. Introduction
Data rate and channel capacity requirements have been
extensively studied in recent years for high-rate data
communication in [1, 2]. In the domain of short-range
wireless technologies that require high data rates, the
unlicensed ultrawideband (UWB) (3.1–10.6 GHz) spec-
trum is signifcantly favorable. Nevertheless, the limitations
of UWB antenna, such as multiple paths’ fading, diminish
its advantages for its use in wireless networks [3–5]. Te
combination of multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO)
technology with UWB antenna systems is a highly efcient
strategy for enhancing the data rate within the same
channel [6]. Consequently, the UWB MIMO antennas ofer
improved channel capacity and increased throughput.
Notwithstanding the numerous benefts obtained with
MIMO antennas in contemporary communication sys-
tems, there are still certain problems linked to them. Te
contiguous placement of several antennas on a common
ground surface leads to signifcant current coupling

between the antennas, which in turn reduces the MIMO

Various methods have been documented in the liter-
ature for achieving enhanced isolation. Tese methods
include the use of defective ground structures [6–10],
decoupling networks [11, 12], space diversity [13], parasitic
elements [14–18], neutralization lines [19, 20], hybrids
[21–24], shorting pins [25], and metamaterials [26–28].
DGS have been extensively used in the literature to improve
mutual coupling [6–10]. Additionally, the use of branches
with modifed rectangular stubs on the ground plane has
been described [6], and connecting partial ground and its
four extended branches has shown to improve isolation
[12]. Furthermore, polarization and space diversity have
been used to minimize electromagnetic interference [13].
Kumar et al. have proposed several parasitic elements’
designs to obtain better isolation in MIMO systems [15]. A
unique E-shaped element between the antenna has shown
to achieve isolation [16]. In MIMO systems, the neutrali-
zation line enhances isolation among elements by pro-
viding neutralizing current to the mutual current. Kumar
et al. utilized a neutralization line, which includes a hori-
zontal stub connecting the radiator, to enhance isolation
across the impedance bandwidth [17]. Additionally, to
reduce mutual coupling between MIMO antenna struc-
tures, a defective ground plane and four defective feed lines
have been introduced [22]. A hybrid strategy employing
three grounded parasitic elements and a mirrored F-shaped
defective ground surface between the two patches is pro-
posed in [24] as an additional method to enhance the
MIMO antenna isolation. High isolation has been achieved
in [26–28] by utilizing various types of metamaterial
structures. Te researchers presented a semifexible two-
element MIMO system for wearables in [29]. Te reso-
nating frequency was achieved via sectoral slots on the
patch and moon-shaped ground surface slots.
While earlier studies showed the efcacy of many UWB
MIMO antennas, thus designing a small and efcient UWB
MIMO radiator poses a signifcant challenge in achieving de-
sired isolation levels. Tis paper outlines the design of a new
UWB MIMO structure employing a FR4 substrate. Te antenna
has been carefully designed to operate precisely in the frequency
band of 4.6 to 13.6GHz. Te antenna has measurements of
21.5× 34×1.6mm3. Enhanced impedance matching of the
circular monopole patch is achieved by including an elliptical
stub into the radiator and minimizing the ground surface area.
Te implementation of a caterpillar-shaped stub between the
elements yields isolation levels above 20dB. Furthermore, the
MIMO diversity parameters of the proposed antenna were
assessed. Further detailed explanations of the antenna’s design
are provided in the subsequent sections.
2. Antenna Design
In order to attain UWB operating frequency, the circular
monopole radiator is altered by incorporating an ellipse
between the feedline and patch. To expand the bandwidth of
the UWB antenna element, a supplementary rectangular cut
is included into the partial ground surface. A FR4 substrate
with a dielectric constant of 4.4, a loss tangent of 0.002, and
a thickness of 1.6 mm is used to design the radiator. In order
to fabricate a dual-port MIMO antenna, the UWB elements
are arranged with a 10-mm gap between each component, as
shown in Figure 1. Te isolation problems demonstrated in
Figures 2 and 3 are due to the spatial distance among UWB
elements, which are less than 1/4 of the wavelength. Te
isolation curve in Figure 3 illustrates that the current cou-
pling among the MIMO elements is adequately low at lower
frequency ranges. To improve the isolation at lower fre-
quencies, a parasitic caterpillar-shaped stub is positioned
among the elements of the MIMO, as shown in Figure 4.
Side-by-side radiating elements are isolated from one
another by the parasitic stub in the shape of a caterpillar that
is positioned between the radiators. Figure 4 depicts the
decoupling structure. By acting as transmission line reso-
nators, these top-side strips efciently lessen the mutual
coupling between the radiating parts that are adjacent to
each other. Between adjacent antennas, decoupling per-
formance greater than 20 dB is attained. Te calculated
measurements of the designed MIMO structure are pre-
sented in Table 1. Te entire MIMO system measurement
measured to be 21.5 × 34 ×1.6 mm3. Te inductor–capacitor
(LC) tank circuit is utilized to imitate port-to-port coupling.
Te enhanced isolation is attained through the band stop
features, which create transmission zeros inside the an-
tenna’s working frequency. Te equivalent circuit of the
antenna with a decoupling structure is shown in Figure 5.
3. Results and Discussion
Te measured and simulation operation of the designed
UWB MIMO system is presented in this section. To realize
a signifcant degree of precision between the observed and
tested data, and to improve the design, Ansoft HFSS sim-
ulators are extensively employed. A range of metrics, in-
cluding radiation characteristics and MIMO diversity
parameters, are assessed and examined to ascertain the ef-
fcacy of the antenna design. Figure 6 illustrates the pro-
totype of the designed radiator.
Figure 7 illustrates the simulated and observed values of
S11 and isolation (S21) for the antenna that was developed. Te
antenna’s impedance bandwidth is observed to range from 4.6
to 13.6GHz. Additionally, it accomplishes a level of isolation
that surpasses 20dB throughout its entire operating bandwidth.
Figure 8 illustrates the surface currents at 5.6 and 11.1GHz.
To study the impact of radiation, one antenna element is ac-
tivated to emit the radiation, while the other elements are
stopped at a matching impedance. Te presence of the parasitic
element located between elements in the MIMO antenna
functions as a flter, hence reduces mutual coupling.
Te normalized radiation pattern of the MIMO antenna
is displayed in the E- and H-planes for resonance frequencies
of 5.6 and 11.1 GHz. Figure 9 shows the copolarization and
cross-polarization radiation patterns at these frequencies.
Te radiation pattern in the E-plane is bidirectional, while in
the H-plane, it has omnidirectional radiation.

simulation and measurement. Te antenna exhibits a gain of

Using the MIMO technology in wireless data commu-
nication adds an additional level of fexibility and signif-
cantly boosts data bandwidth [30]. Tese systems make use
of several antennas to take advantage of diferent channels
and propagation paths. Te mixed signals from various
antennas can be processed separately at the receiving end.
MIMO systems increase their performance and efciency
with less correlated received signals, resulting in improved
performance.

4. Conclusion
Tis study suggests the development of a two-port UWB
MIMO antenna that is both compact and low profle. Te
measured results verify its ability to encompass a wide
frequency spectrum, including the UWB spectrum. Te
UWB antenna arrangement is created by incorporating an
elliptical shape into a circular monopole patch. To further
improve the bandwidth, a square-shaped slot is incorporated
into the partial ground surface. A unique caterpillar-shaped
parasitic element between the antennas is incorporated to
achieve isolation above 20 dB. Te MIMO antenna has
a bandwidth that ranges from 4.6 to 13.6 GHz. Te analysis
encompasses the evaluation of performance features, in-
cluding the refection and isolation coefcient curves, far-
feld radiation characteristics, surface current distribution,
and MIMO diversity parameter (ECC, DG, MEG, TARC,
and CCL). In the future, devices will be employed for routine
activities and overall wellness in sectors such as healthcare,
telemedicine, defense, sports, entertainment, and search-
and-rescue operations. Owing to these essential character-
istics, a wearable antenna is expected to be fexible, compact,
afordable, lightweight, energy-efcient, low-power, porta-
ble, readily accessible, adaptable for integration, and capable
of high data rates and advanced wireless communication.
